output.headline: Brand's conviction prompts ministers to review rape myths in court
output.bodyHtml:
Russell Brand’s convictions for rape and sexual assault have prompted ministers to look again at how rape trials are conducted, as police investigate reports that at least 10 more women may have been attacked by the disgraced star.

The fallout from Brand’s case has already seen the government pledge to examine calls to crack down on “rape myths” in trials.

A No 10 source said the prime minister, Andy Burnham, believed calls from the victims’ commissioner, Claire Waxman, for a legal duty that would require judges to issue directions to juries on rape myths and misconceptions, should be examined.

A Ministry of Justice spokesperson said: “Rape myths have absolutely no place in our courts and victims should never feel as though they are the ones on trial.

“Judges are already able to give directions to counter rape myths … we will also carefully consider the victims’ commissioner’s proposals as we continue to strengthen protections for victims.”

Siobhan Blake, the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) lead for rape and serious sexual offences, said: “The focus must be the actions of the perpetrator and not the behaviour of the victim.

“We know that there is no typical response to sexual assault and myths that victims should scream and fight back are outdated. Some people may freeze or feel unable to speak about it for months or even years, but this is not a barrier to justice.”

Burnham told Times Radio: “It’s horrifying what Russell Brand has done. And I’d firstly like to praise the bravery of the women, the victims in the case, who’ve come forward and had the courage to speak out.

“But yes, the journalists too, who supported those who had been abused by Russell Brand. So all of them deserve our praise for having that courage to come forward.”

Burnham told Times Radio he will look at making changes to rape trials so that they “do not leave the woman feeling like she is on trial.”

He said: “We need to constantly look at the way rape trials are conducted to make sure that they do not leave the woman feeling like she is on trial in court, as has been the experience of people in the past … we need to encourage more women to come forward to report rape.”

Later on the BBC, Burnham was asked about a statement of support for Brand in 2014 as the star faced media criticism, and said: “Well, over a decade ago, and all I can say is I had no idea of the full extent of what he was doing or what he went on to do. His crimes are horrific.”

Police are bracing themselves for more victims of Russell Brand to come forward. The Guardian understands that next week the Metropolitan police team that built the case against Brand will start sifting through reports and intelligence about other potential victims.

The Met commissioner, Sir Mark Rowley, said there could be “many more” victims, but declined to say how many, with some intelligence about further victims being third-hand and some further suspected victims reluctant to face the criminal justice system.

Sources say it is feared the number of further victims is at least in “double digits”, with 10 currently seen as a minimum.

The Met police said on Thursday that Brand was under investigation for two further rape allegations. Detectives have sent files to specialist rape prosecutors and are in discussions with them over the material.

Rowley said: “We’ve got two other victims who’ve come forward who want to tell their story, and so two rape cases we’re investigating. I wouldn’t be surprised if many, many more come forward, and we’re open to that.”

Rowley declined on LBC Radio to confirm the new allegations would reach “double figures”, and said: “I’m not going to guess on this, but we’ve seen in the past with high-profile individuals who are brought to justice that it does often bring out a flood of other cases. Let’s see where this one goes.”

Brand’s trial, which spanned claims of attacks from 1999 to 2009, saw women asked by the defence barrister why they had not screamed during attacks.

Brand, 51, will be sentenced on Monday to what is expected to be a lengthy jail sentence for rape and sexual assaults after he abused his fame to become a “predator” targeting women, and got away with it for years.

Brand now faces years of imprisonment and the growing prospect of a fresh trial over further allegations.

He was convicted on Thursday of raping a young fan at his luxury London townhouse in 2009, continuing despite her pleas for him to stop. He had picked her out of a crowd. He was also found guilty of sexually assaulting three women in separate incidents at a radio station, a recording studio and a bar.

Victims are expected to tell of the impact his crimes had on them in court on Monday.

Brand became an international star, acting in Hollywood films, and in latter years an online influencer, but was dogged by whispers and allegations about his danger to women. He was accused of treating women as a “disposable commodity” and a “means to an end” to satisfy his voracious sexual appetite.

The government says it is committed to reducing violence against women and girls by half.

The comedian Katherine Ryan, who warned of a “predator” in the entertainment industry before Brand’s trial, said she felt relief at his conviction.

“They came forward despite Russell Brand having fame, power, money and a legion of fans ready to attack them,” she said.

“I will never be someone who, like, dances on graves. There has been some justice done today. There’s a level of relief, but there’s grief alongside relief.”

Bear Grylls, who baptised Brand when he converted to Christianity in 2024, said the star’s faith seemed genuine and added: “It is right that justice has now been served. I can’t imagine how hard this time has been for the victims, the heroes of the day.”

Brand was cleared of two further charges of rape and one allegation of attempted indecent assault.

Brand’s victims told how he “snapped” – changing from charming to nasty – as he raped and sexually assaulted them before gaslighting them into believing nothing was wrong.
output.standfirst: Russell Brand's convictions for rape and sexual assault have prompted ministers to consider a legal duty on rape myths in court, as police investigate reports that at least 10 more women may have been attacked.
output.progress: Ministers say they will consider a legal duty requiring judges to challenge rape myths in court, following calls from the victims' commissioner.

output.headline: Miller's appointment galvanises Democrats to fight Trump's agenda
output.bodyHtml:
Stephen Miller, Donald Trump’s most controversial aide and the architect of his sweeping immigration enforcement drive, will become his new White House chief of staff days after Republicans lost control of the US Congress in US midterm elections.

The president announced the extraordinary appointment on Friday, confirming that Susie Wiles – his current chief of staff, and the first woman to serve in the role – had been ousted.

A growing chorus of Democrats condemned the appointment and said they were ready to fight it. Hakeem Jeffries, who is poised to become the first Black speaker of the House, posted: “Stephen Miller is a dangerous xenophobe and reckless extremist who has American blood on his hands. His presence in government should be eradicated like a malignant tumor. Fire him today.”

Chuck Schumer, likely to be the next majority leader of the Senate, wrote: “Donald Trump learned nothing from his historic defeat. Stephen Miller is the architect of the most barbaric, inhumane policies of this administration. Trump couldn’t have made a worse choice. Our Democratic majorities will fight him every step of the way.”

In a social media post, Trump called Miller, 41, “one of my most trusted advisors” and praised Wiles for doing “an outstanding job”. Miller will begin on Monday.

Wiles, 69, reportedly handed in her resignation on Thursday night and said in a social media post that serving Trump “has been the honor of a lifetime”.

Holding an umbrella, Trump emerged from the White House South Portico on Friday for a trip to Florida. “I wanted to make a change,” he said. “I think Susie’s done a very good job ... Stephen’s been great, and we’ve got to make moves.”

“Stephen’s been with me from the beginning. He gets it,” the president said. “Very good politically and he’s a very good man. He’ll do a great job. Great manager.”

Related: Republicans hoping to succeed Trump in 2028 dissect midterm rout

Trump then boarded the Marine One helicopter, followed by Miller, secretary of state Marco Rubio and close aide Natalie Harp.

In a statement, Wiles added: “I’m so proud to have been a part of what we’ve accomplished together from securing our border and cutting taxes to strengthening our economy and putting America First.”

She said her commitment to “the President and the mission” will not change.

Miller posted on X that he was “honored beyond words” to serve as Trump’s chief of staff. He added: “The mission now is more clear than ever: Fight with all of our soul to support our President and defend this magnificent Republic.”

Miller’s appointment is the first sign of a shake-up at the White House following Republicans’ catastrophic defeat in the midterms. His record as a far-right firebrand implies that Trump is preparing for an aggressive fight against congressional Democrats’ oversight and investigations.

Chris Whipple, author of The Gatekeepers: How the White House Chiefs of Staff Define Every Presidency, told CNN: “It’s almost a declaration of war by Trump … He [Miller] only knows one gear and that’s full-throttle, full steam ahead over the cliff.”

David Axelrod, a veteran Democratic strategist, added on X: “For those who hoped the @POTUS might pivot to work with the incoming Congress, the appointment of Miller is a bucket of ICE cold water.”

Miller is one of the most polarising figures in the administration and one of Trump’s closest and longest-serving advisers, having joined his 2016 presidential campaign as a speechwriter. He is a former aide to the former senator Jeff Sessions of Alabama, who would go on to serve as Trump’s first attorney general.

In Trump’s first term, Miller was the driving force behind policies such as family separation and a travel ban on Muslim-majority countries. More than a hundred Democrats in Congress signed a letter to Trump calling Miller a “documented white nationalist” and demanding his removal.

A biography of Miller, written by journalist Jean Guerrero in 2020, was entitled Hatemonger.

Miller has served as deputy chief of staff since Trump’s return to the presidency in January 2025. He had been hugely influential in hardline immigration policies and demanding an end to birthright citizenship. He is also one Trump’s most ardent, outspoken and pugnacious defenders.

Appearing on Sean Hannity’s Fox News show on Monday, just before the midterms, Miller said of the president: “He saved America from a corrupt political class. He saved America from open borders. He saved America from countries that want the American way of life to end, from foreign adversaries, from domestic adversaries.”

Miller added: “President Trump took a bullet for you, he bled for you, he faced life in prison for you. And what he needs from you tomorrow is your vote.”

Wiles is the longest-serving White House chief of staff for Trump, who cycled through four of them during his first four-year term.

Wiles led Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign to victory and was credited with bringing discipline to a chaotic effort and clamping down on leaks from his second administration.

Related: Two more DoJ officials resign, including US attorney leading inquiry into Trump rivals

The Florida operative generally shunned the limelight. At Trump’s 2024 election night victory party, she repeatedly shook her head and avoided the microphone as Trump tried to coax her to speak to the crowd.

But Wiles made headlines last year when Vanity Fair magazine published a series of interviews with her and other top Trump administration officials. Her comments stood out for their candour, including her observation that Trump has an “alcoholic’s personality”.

Her departure came months after she indicated she no longer showed evidence of breast cancer after she underwent months of treatment for the disease. She went public with the diagnosis in March.

Critics said Miller’s appointment showed that Trump had learned the wrong lessons from Tuesday’s electoral reckoning.

Becca Balint, a Democratic congresswoman from Vermont, posted on X: “On Tuesday, the American people rose up and overwhelmingly voted in opposition to the disgusting and inhumane policies of this second Trump administration. What does Trump do? He promotes Stephen Miller – the architect of some of this administration’s worst decisions. Sickening.”

Anthony Scaramucci, who had a brief spell as White House communications director during Trump’s first term, tweeted: “Trump saw the midterm results and decided elevating Stephen Miller is the answer. 🤣 He is even more delusional than I thought. Or maybe he actually wants to finish destroying the @GOP? 🤔”
output.standfirst:
Donald Trump has named Stephen Miller, architect of his hardline immigration policy, as his new chief of staff, prompting Democratic congressional leaders to vow fierce opposition to his agenda.

  • US politics live – latest updates
output.progress: Democratic leaders including Hakeem Jeffries and Chuck Schumer say they will use their incoming majorities in Congress to resist Miller's agenda.

output.headline: Philippines inquiry led FBI to Florida arrest of Meghan's father
output.bodyHtml:
Thomas Markle, the father of Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, was arrested by US federal agents in Florida on Friday and charged in connection with possession of child sexual abuse material, according to the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), after an investigation that traced back to developments in the Philippines.

The director of the FBI, Kash Patel, said: “Mr Markle allegedly targeted innocent children and sought to steal their innocence through his criminal actions. This FBI will use every single resource at our disposal to protect innocent kids – any predator who targets children will have zero safe haven in this country or anywhere they try to hide.”

Patel thanked FBI agents in Los Angeles and Tampa, and authorities in Mexico, the Philippines, and Marshall Islands that he said were involved in the investigation.

“Mr Markle is accused of possessing child sexual abuse material, including photographs depicting himself with minor girls,” Bill Essayli, first assistant US attorney for the central district of California, said in a statement released by the US department of justice.

“These allegations are extremely serious, and we will prosecute Mr Markle to the fullest extent of federal law.”

Markle, 82, was taken into custody at a senior care facility in Polk county early on Friday, and made a brief initial appearance in federal court in Tampa on Friday afternoon, the Associated Press reported. He was later released with the condition that he be electronically monitored.

A 14-page federal criminal complaint says that agents seized approximately 78 items and alleges that Markle kept child sexual abuse material, including sexually explicit photographs of himself with prepubescent girls, in two Los Angeles-area storage units that he rented for nearly two decades.

An affidavit filed with the complaint that led to the arrest stated that two of the images inside the units showed a man identified by a witness as Markle with a nude underage girl.

The document, filed in federal court in California, said the recovered material included dozens of slides, photographs, film negatives and books containing the illegal material. It said the FBI was still reviewing the material.

Some details in the criminal complaint are redacted, such as the name of the federal agent who signed the complaint, who states that they are assigned to the violent crimes against children unit in the LA office of the FBI. The case is presented as United States of America v Thomas Wayne Markle.

Essayli told the Associated Press that there was no evidence of victims in the US, based on the seized material, but that the investigation was ongoing. He said his office was aware of public reporting that Markle might have dementia.

Markle is charged with one count of possession of child sexual abuse material, and faces up to 20 years in federal prison if convicted.

Efforts by the AP to reach Markle’s court-appointed lawyer for comment were unsuccessful, the news agency said.

According to the justice department statement, FBI agents interviewed a person last month who was aware that Markle was renting the two storage units in California after the bureau became aware of developments in the Philippines.

Markle rented the units since 2008, it said, with his most recent payments on both made last month by auto-pay.

Authorities in the Philippines, where Markle had previously lived for some time, began investigating him last month over allegations he possessed child sexual abuse images. British police last month said they would refer allegations about him to overseas law enforcement agencies after finding that claims had not been passed to other authorities when they were first received.

Meghan, the wife of Prince Harry, said last month that she was “deeply distressed” about allegations that a collection of child sexual abuse images was found at her father’s former home in the Philippines.

The duchess also revealed that a letter containing “troubling allegations” about her father was sent to police in London in 2018.

She had issued a statement after the Sun newspaper published claims that her half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr, alleged he had found a stash of images belonging to their father at his Philippines residence. He was named as a person of interest in the case earlier this week.

Photographs produced by the Daily Mail showed Thomas Markle Sr being taken away in a wheelchair, in handcuffs, wearing a black T-shirt and surrounded by agents wearing jackets marked “FBI”. The UK tabloid asked Markle if he was a pedophile and he replied: “No.” Markle did not answer when the newspaper asked if he had ever collected child sexual abuse material.

A spokesperson for the duchess did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

He has denied the accusations, telling the Daily Mail they were untrue and “sick lies”.

Markle is a retired television lighting and photography director and he did not attend the 2018 wedding of Harry and Meghan, amid acrimony and estrangement between father and daughter. Meghan has since said she decided to distance herself from him to protect her children.

The duke and duchess returned to live in Britain in the summer after six years in the US.

The Associated Press and Reuters contributed reporting

  • In the US, call or text the Childhelp abuse hotline on 800-422-4453 or visit their website for more resources and to report child abuse or DM for help. For adult survivors of child abuse, help is available at ascasupport.org. In the UK, the NSPCC offers support to children on 0800 1111, and adults concerned about a child on 0808 800 5000. The National Association for People Abused in Childhood (Napac) offers support for adult survivors on 0808 801 0331. In Australia, children, young adults, parents and teachers can contact the Kids Helpline on 1800 55 1800, or Bravehearts on 1800 272 831, and adult survivors can contact Blue Knot Foundation on 1300 657 380. Other sources of help can be found at Child Helplines International
output.standfirst: FBI agents arrested Thomas Markle, the father of the Duchess of Sussex, in Florida after an investigation that traced back to developments in the Philippines, and charged him with possessing child sexual abuse material, including images of himself with underage girls.
output.progress: The FBI's violent crimes against children unit pursued the case after the bureau was alerted by developments in a Philippines investigation into Markle.

output.headline: Strong US jobs growth lifts Wall Street as tech shares rebound
output.bodyHtml:
European and Asian stock markets fell sharply on Friday, a day after the Democrats’ decisive victory in the midterms triggered a rout in US tech stocks that later eased as Wall Street reopened.

Tech stocks rose on Wall Street on Friday, lifting the S&P 500 by 0.3% and the Nasdaq by 1%, as signs of easing jitters emerged – though the gains recovered only a portion of the previous day’s losses.

A stronger-than-expected employment report helped drive the recovery: the US economy added 165,000 new jobs in October, pulling the unemployment rate down to 4.1%.

Despite the sharp losses, most indices remain up for the year: the Nasdaq Composite is still up 6.35% since the start of January, even though it is more than 10% below its peak.

The FTSE 100 has gained almost 7.5% in 2026, though it remains more than 300 points below the record high it set in July.

Mohit Kumar, an economist at the investment bank Jefferies, said he did not believe Thursday’s losses marked the “start of the unwind of the AI trade”, even though he did not expect a quick rebound in the US.

He said: “AI investment has been a key driver of US growth and we do not see the Democrats as giving up on this growth engine. Datacentres and AI infrastructure also create jobs and Democrats would be reluctant to let those jobs move on to other states or outside the country.”

A sell-off on Wall Street on Thursday was followed by sharp falls in Asian stock markets on Friday, with the pressure then reaching London, where the market was at one stage poised for its worst day since March.

The FTSE 100 index, which tracks blue-chip shares listed in London, was down as much as 254 points, or 2.35%, at 10,528 points during a wave of selling in morning trading, but clawed back some of its losses to close down 1%, helped by a rise in US stocks when Wall Street reopened.

Germany’s Dax index fell by 2%, France’s Cac 40 dropped by 0.8% and Spain’s Ibex lost 0.6%.

Susannah Streeter, the chief investment strategist at Wealth Club, said: “The tech sell-off has intensified, with the pain of the brutal sell-off on Wall Street carried straight through to Asia and knocking sentiment in Europe.

“Big worries are colliding – the build-out of datacentres looks set to slow, which risks shredding the spending spree underpinning the boom, right at the time that investors have become super nervous about returns on this massive investment.”

On Thursday, the Nasdaq share index had its worst day in 19 months after slumping 5.5%.

Chip stocks led the slump on Thursday, with the memory maker SanDisk tumbling by 22% and the hard drive maker Western Digital falling by 17%. Wall Street’s “fear index”, the Vix, jumped by more than 60% to its highest levels since the early weeks of the Iran war, in a sign of rising market volatility.

The heavy falls continued in Asia on Friday, with Japan’s Nikkei 225 index sinking 6% and South Korea’s Kospi index tumbling more than 6.5%.

“It’s actually a bit of a disaster,” said Christopher Forbes, the head of Asia and Middle East at CMC Markets.

“[Clients] were long index, long stocks, and they all got carried out. All night, all day – we had client margin calls, client complaints … because it’s a very emotional thing, right? People are wedded to their positions and views on a stock or outcome, and you’re telling them: ‘Look, you’ve just lost money.’”

Chris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, said: “Yesterday’s [Thursday’s] brutal session marked a dramatic turnaround from Wednesday, but with AI fears still prominent there is a risk that there is much more selling to come.

“Investors remain on watch for a potential resumption of the Iran conflict, and are nervously watching the oil price after its slump earlier in the week. All in all it remains a very febrile atmosphere.”

Stock market tremors have also hit the London Metal Exchange, with copper poised for its biggest weekly fall since March.

Benchmark three-month copper, a key metal used in the semiconductor, electronics and automotive industry, has dropped 0.61%, leaving it positioned for a 2.79% fall this week.

Craig Lang, a principal analyst at the consultancy CRU, said the price of copper was increasingly influenced by the AI market and “sentiment towards datacentre expansion”.
output.standfirst: A stronger-than-expected US jobs report helped steady Wall Street on Friday, after concerns over AI spending drove sharp falls across European and Asian markets, with Tokyo’s Nikkei down 6% and Seoul’s Kospi down more than 6.5%.
output.progress: US tech stocks rose on Friday, with the Nasdaq closing up 1%, as a stronger jobs report eased investor nerves.

output.headline: Two charged and remanded in custody over Waterford fire investigation
output.bodyHtml:
Two people have been charged and remanded in custody over a fire in Waterford that has killed five members of one family, after a six-year-old boy became the third child in the family to die from his injuries, Gardaí have said.

Elliot English died on Friday at Children’s Health Ireland hospital in Crumlin from injuries sustained in the 13 October fire in the Birchwood area of Waterford city.

His parents, Kim and Philip English, and their sons, Callum, 12, and Jayden, nine, were also killed. Another child remains in a critical condition.

In October, Jessica Dalton, 31, and Cian Stacey, 21, appeared in court charged in relation to the attack, with one count of criminal damage and two counts of assault causing serious harm, and were remanded into custody. They will appear before Waterford district court on 17 November via video link.

A Garda Síochána spokesperson said: “The thoughts of all members of An Garda Síochána are with the extended English family at this sad time.”

In a statement reported by RTÉ, the family confirmed the passing of Elliot with “profound sadness”.

They said: “This comes following the tragic events in Birchwood [ …] in which Elliot’s mother, Kim, his father, Philip, and his two brothers, Jaden and Callum, tragically lost their lives.

“The family has endured an unimaginable loss, and this latest bereavement has left relatives, neighbours and friends facing an overwhelming period of grief.

“At this incredibly difficult time, the family respectfully asks members of the media to allow them, along with their neighbours and friends, the time, space and privacy to come to terms with this devastating tragedy.”

The family said their thoughts remain with the child who remains in hospital, who they asked be “kept in everyone’s thoughts and prayers”.

Last week, a man arrested in connection with the fire was released without charge. He was the sixth person to have been arrested in connection with the incident.
output.standfirst: Jessica Dalton, 31, and Cian Stacey, 21, are due in court on 17 November charged with criminal damage and assault, after a fire that has now killed five members of one family, including six-year-old Elliot English, who died on Friday, with another child still critical.
output.progress: Jessica Dalton and Cian Stacey have been charged with criminal damage and assault causing serious harm, due in court on 17 November.

output.headline: Prince Harry leads bid to overturn Daily Mail privacy ruling
output.bodyHtml:
Prince Harry and five other prominent figures have launched a legal challenge against a judge’s verdict in their unsuccessful claims against the Daily Mail’s publisher, Associated Newspapers.

Harry, Doreen Lawrence, the mother of the murdered black teenager Stephen Lawrence, the singer Elton John and his husband, David Furnish, and the actors Elizabeth Hurley and Sadie Frost, are challenging the ruling after facing a legal bill of more than £50m when they lost their case claiming that Mail journalists used unlawful methods to source stories.

In an unequivocal ruling in July, Mr Justice Nicklin dismissed their case, stating that the claimants had not proved any information had been obtained unlawfully.

His 436-page written verdict, after an 11-week trial, said it could not be inferred that a story had been obtained unlawfully if there remained a legitimate and realistic legal way in which it could have been sourced.

In a statement issued on Friday, a spokesperson for Harry and his five fellow claimants said: “We confirm that the claimants have today filed applications with the court of appeal for permission to appeal the judgments of Mr Justice Nicklin in respect of his dismissal of their claims and the indemnity costs order.

“The claimants respectfully disagree with those unprecedented decisions, which they consider to be legally and factually flawed.”

Court staff confirmed on Friday that an application to appeal against the rulings had been filed at the court of appeal.

Barristers for the claimants had alleged during the trial that private investigators, freelance journalists and staff at Associated Newspapers had carried out acts including voicemail interception, landline tapping and obtaining information by deception, also known as “blagging”.

But lawyers for the publisher said Daily Mail and Mail on Sunday journalists had provided a “compelling account of a pattern of legitimate sourcing of articles”, including friends and “leaky” social circles, press officers and spokespeople, as well as previous reporting, freelance journalists and stories from other newspapers and news agencies.

Associated’s legal team described the claims as “lurid” and “preposterous”.

After the verdict the former Mail editor Paul Dacre said the case was a “conspiracy” orchestrated by press regulation campaigners to “destroy a paper”.

Harry and Lawrence said the verdict was a “complete and obvious whitewash”. They added: “When the court says there is not sufficient evidence of wrongdoing … then one does wonder how justice was ever going to be achieved.”

In August, Nicklin ruled that the claimants had to pay £9,544,355 within seven days as an initial contribution to the publisher’s costs before further hearings to determine the total sum.
output.standfirst: Harry, Doreen Lawrence, Elton John and others have filed court of appeal applications against Mr Justice Nicklin’s ruling, after facing a bill of more than £50m for losing their claims that the Daily Mail’s publisher used unlawful information gathering to source stories.
output.progress: Harry and five co-claimants have formally filed applications with the court of appeal challenging the ruling and costs order.

output.headline: Eurovision launches a flamboyant new chapter in Bangkok
output.bodyHtml:
Thailand is about to get a glitz-infused injection of pop culture, with crews starting construction of a large stage in Bangkok as part of an extravagant attempt to transplant Eurovision to Asia.

Organisers have promised the world’s longest-running music competition will launch “a new chapter in Asia” next weekend, when 11 contestants from across the region will sing and dance for votes.

How much notice an Asian audience has shown in the experiment to replicate the beloved contest is yet to be seen, although organisers will hope it sets off a Eurovision-mania chain reaction. Several competitor countries, such as the Philippines and South Korea, already have avid Eurovision fanclubs.

Still, a week before the grand final ample tickets remained on sale for entry to the concert hall at One Bangkok Forum, which sits near the city’s celebrated Lumphini Park.

Eurovision’s official Instagram account has been promoting its Asian sister account to its 2.3m followers. So far, about 65,000 accounts have followed. Bulgaria’s Eurovision 2026 winner, Dara, is getting flown over to perform her electro-dance earworm, Bangaranga, during the interval.

Dean Vuletic, author of Postwar Europe and the Eurovision Song Contest, said the nascent show would face an uphill battle to “capture the attention and fascination of the local audience”.

Vuletic, an academic who taught the world’s first university course on Eurovision, attributed the contest’s extraordinary success in part because it emerged in the late 1950s during the rise of television, and at a period of postwar European integration. “So there’s a reason why Eurovision is peculiarly European, and why I think it would struggle to succeed elsewhere,” he said.

Another spin-off version, titled American Song Contest, received poor viewing figures in 2022, facing stiff competition from more established shows such as American Idol.

Despite his reservations, Vuletic travelled to Thailand for the final show. He said: “This is another chapter in that history that I think I have to see.”

In what appears to be an attempt to hold on to the name association of the world’s largest live music event, the show has not rebranded itself as “Asiavision” but gone with the spin-off title “Eurovision Song Contest Asia”, leading to some geographic confusion.

However, such regional melding is not unusual in Eurovision’s 70-year history. The competition is run by the European Broadcasting Union (EBU), which despite its name is not location-specific, meaning broadcasters outside Europe take part, including those from Israel and Australia. Next year’s Eurovision will feature a Canadian act for the first time.

In the rush to lock down competitors, not all of Asia is covered, with India and China absent. The 11 announced performers are from Bhutan, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Laos, Malaysia, Mongolia, Nepal, the Philippines, South Korea, Thailand and Vietnam.

The hosting nation’s own entrant is a collaboration including a solo female artist and local T-Pop (Thai Pop) star, Mang. She joins Daou, who gained national fame through winning a survival-style Thai TV show and his role in a short-lived boyband called LAZ1.

Anyone in the world can view the live show on YouTube, and even vote, although under a complex voting system their voice will not overrule national juries and public votes in participating countries. Eurovision onlookers have been wondering if political allegiances will affect results, as they have for the main event, where friendly neighbours often appear to engage in bloc voting. Thailand and Cambodia were at war last year, which could play out in the tallies on the night.

Eurovision attracts more than 100 million viewers every year. The competition has been overshadowed by accusations that Israel should be excluded over its war in Gaza. Critics say its continued inclusion is at odds with the banning of Russia after its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, and several broadcasters have pulled out.
output.standfirst: Organisers hope their extravagant attempt to bring the world’s longest-running song contest to Asia will succeed, as acts from 11 countries prepare to compete.

output.headline: Macklemore vows more Free Palestine tour dates after European triumph
output.bodyHtml:
Macklemore says Free Palestine shows will continue, after nine major US arenas refused to host his fundraising tour, among what he called “intimidation, manipulation and suppression” tactics against artists speaking out for Palestinians.

In an Instagram post, Macklemore said he had hoped to bring the tour to the US, but that nine major arenas turned him down, including New York City’s Madison Square Garden, Los Angeles’s Crypto.com arena and Brooklyn’s Barclays Center.

Related: Macklemore’s Free Palestine tour review – a triumph of a show with performances from Hozier, Kneecap and more

Last month, Macklemore brought the Free Palestine tour to Dublin, London and Paris in a show praised by the Guardian’s Alexis Petridis as “a triumph”. The shows came in the wake of Ed Sheeran dropping the rapper from his US tour after he made an onstage speech in support of Palestine.

“From the beginning, our plan was to bring this tour home to the US,” Macklemore wrote. “But after weeks of reaching out, nine major American arenas have turned us down.”

Macklemore said that other venues in the New York tri-state area, including UBS arena and Prudential Center turned him down, as well as Los Angeles’s Intuit Dome and Kia Forum, San Francisco’s Chase Center and Seattle’s Climate Pledge arena.

“By mid-September, we received available dates at these arenas through the end of the year. But once they found out these were my benefit shows for Palestine, those dates were suddenly off the table,” he said.

“The doors were closed. The conversations were all different, but the result was the same. The shows were not going to be allowed to happen in these venues.”

In an impassioned post that spanned seven Instagram slides, Macklemore said that he no longer cared about burning bridges with music industry top dogs.

“The intimidation, manipulation and suppression I experienced are part of how those in power keep entertainers quiet,” he said. “It’s their main tactic to keep us in line. Shut up and dribble, or you will be punished.

“But at this point, I’m three years past giving two shits about maintaining any relationships, business or personal, with anyone that isn’t riding for a Free Palestine.”

After making a brief speech in support of “the occupied West Bank” in early September while opening up for Sheeran, Macklemore was dropped from the tour. Sheeran claimed that US venues told him that they would refuse to host the show if the rapper continued as the tour’s supporting act.

“I am not complicit,” Sheeran said. “I have my personal views on this devastating conflict. Just because I choose not to speak publicly, it doesn’t mean I don’t have them, and it doesn’t mean that I don’t care. Nor does it mean that I don’t support causes in my own, personal way.”

Shortly after, all four opening acts as well as Sheeran’s live band quit the tour in solidarity with Macklemore.

On social media, the rapper said: “I’d rather lose every opportunity in this industry than spend another day protecting people who value their business relationships with Israel more than they value Palestinian human life.

“I dream of a world where saying Free Palestine is not controversial,” he added. “It is expected. Where artists value their freedom of speech and collective liberation more than their brand deals.

“Look at what just happened in Europe,” he went on, referring to his shows in Dublin, Paris and London. “Three sold-out arenas. Tens of thousands of people from different backgrounds, religions and walks of life standing together. More than forty artists and speakers putting their names and platforms behind Palestinian liberation. For all the attempts to paint this movement as one rooted in hatred, what filled those rooms was love.”

Macklemore went on to say that the political mood of the US was changing in the wake of the Democrats sweeping the midterm elections this week.

“The tides are turning,” he wrote. “Just three nights ago, Abdul El-Sayed won his Senate race on a platform that included ending the genocide in Gaza and stopping U.S. arms sales to Israel. AIPAC spent $42m trying to defeat him. And they still couldn’t win.

“The trouble with buying power is believing you’ve bought the people too. The billionaires depend on our silence and complicity. They forget that we buy their tickets. We fill their arenas. We build their empires. And we have the power to bring them down.”

The rapper closed his statement with a promise that more shows in support of Palestine will follow.

“There will be more shows for Palestine,” he said. “We’ll keep working with other artists and organizers, continuing where we left off in Europe. We’ll probably just take that shit outside where it belonged in the first place.

“Our commitment to raising funds and standing in solidarity with the Palestinian people remains the same.”

As an ending note, he said: “They may own the arenas. But they do not own the people who fill them. And they never will. FREE PALESTINE.”
output.standfirst: The rapper’s sold-out European shows for Free Palestine were hailed as ‘a triumph’; he says nine major US arenas have since turned him down for his planned US tour, calling it ‘intimidation, manipulation and suppression’.

output.headline: Researcher cracks the mystery behind Apple’s hidden ‘grey list’
output.bodyHtml:
The “grey list” was found by the independent researcher Derik Kauffman, whose other projects include using AI to find errors in scientific papers. After noticing that he had problems typing certain phrases – but not others – on his iPhone, Kauffman was able to unearth a table containing the list, encoded in Apple’s operating system.

New research shows that Apple has a “grey list” of more than 100,000 words and phrases that it has restricted from being completed by its predictive text.

“Australia is a very bad place to question your sexuality on MDMA with NSA spies” might be a text you would wish to send to your friends, if you have had an extraordinarily complicated night out in Sydney.

But your iPhone won’t help you spell any of it if you try to swipe-type it – that is, by gliding a finger across a keyboard as opposed to pecking out a word.

So if a user wishes to type phrases such as “Dictator Trump”, “NSA spies” or, surprisingly, “Australia is a very bad place”, “question your sexuality” or “on MDMA”, they will have to spell them out.

Apple’s predictive text will not suggest these words. And, if a user attempts to swipe-type them, they will often stumble, changing “United Ireland” to “United Iceland”, for example, or “Tibetan independence” to “Tibetan independences”.

The list he found includes some unsurprising words and phrases. Apple’s iPhone will not autocomplete references to drugs, sexual acts and, perhaps in the spirit of corporate protection, “iMessage isn’t working”.

But it also includes possibly politically charged phrases, which Kauffman described to Reuters as a “light-touch form of censorship”. Among these are “Trayvon Martin”, the name of the Black teenager shot in Florida in 2012, “Kashmir dispute”, “Muslim extremist” and “male chauvinist pig”.

In Hebrew, Apple will not autocomplete the phrase “the occupied territories”. In Arabic, it will not autocomplete the phrase “the Hamas movement”.

The list is one more glimpse into the dark bowels of how autocorrect – the chirpy keyboard partner that helps you look more educated to your loved ones – actually works.

The technology has taken many forms. In its earliest version, Unix, an operating system, would look up each word a user typed against a table of words, to determine if this word was spelled correctly.

Related: Apple warns of ‘unprecedented’ rise in memory chip prices

This evolved into n-grams, a tool which allows an operating system to statistically predict what words might come next, based on the words before it. These form the basis of Apple’s familiar autocorrect, which was known to change expletives into prudish alternatives: “fork” and “ducking”, among other gaffes.

Last year, Apple launched a new autocorrect – a “transformer-based” system that was more akin to an LLM. Reddit sleuths saw this as a possible reason behind a spate of avant-garde spelling suggestions their iPhones made last year.

This hard-coded list illuminates one longstanding mystery behind the world’s spelling coach. Others remain, such as a brief glitch in which users of the dictation feature saw the name “Trump” flash across their screen when they spoke the word “racist” into their iPhones – which Apple quickly remedied.

Apple said that it designed its keyboard to avoid offering inappropriate or offensive predictive suggestions. It said iPhone users could always type out specific words or phrases, and override predictive text suggestions to achieve their desired meaning.
output.standfirst: Independent researcher Derik Kauffman uncovers a hidden table of more than 100,000 words and phrases that Apple’s predictive text won’t complete, including politically sensitive terms he says amount to a light-touch form of censorship.
output.progress: Apple says it designed its keyboard to avoid offensive suggestions, and that users can always type restricted words manually.
